The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2021-02-15.236.1) moved by West Australian Senator [Louise Pratt](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/louise_pratt) (Labor), which means they failed. The amendments related to: * an advance payment scheme for elderly and ill applicants; * a funders of last resort guarantee; * psychological counselling and support; * better recognising the impact of sexual abuse; and * requiring non -participating institutions to contribute to scheme.

The speaker argued that the National Redress Scheme is failing survivors, with only 4,620 payments made out of an estimated 60,000 eligible survivors, and proposed Labor amendments including raising the maximum payment to $200,000, removing indexation of prior payments, making the government a funder of last resort for ineligible institutions, providing ongoing psychological counselling, and creating an advance payment scheme for elderly and unwell survivors.

The member for Oxley argued the National Redress Scheme amendments are insufficient and proposed increasing the maximum payment to $200,000, ensuring prior payments are not deducted, introducing advanced payments for elderly and ill applicants, and requiring institutions that do not join the scheme within 12 months to be publicly named and lose Commonwealth funding.

Labor will move amendments to the National Redress Scheme, including a levy on organisations that refuse to join, an advance payment scheme for elderly or ill survivors, an increase in the redress cap from $150,000 to $200,000, and guaranteed ongoing psychological counselling. The speech also noted that as of 15 January 2021, only 4,660 applications had been finalised out of 9,232 lodged, and named institutions such as the Australian Air League, Jehovah's Witnesses, and the Boys Brigade that have not indicated they will join the scheme.

The speaker argued that the Commonwealth must act as the funder of last resort for survivors of the Retta Dixon Home in Darwin, where Aboriginal children were forcibly taken and abused, because at least 10 survivors remain in limbo after the organisation AIM was barred from the National Redress Scheme due to insufficient funds. The speaker called for an early payment scheme for elderly and ill applicants and noted that the Prime Minister has not responded to a letter on the issue.

The speaker supported the National Redress Scheme Amendment Bill 2020 but called for expedited amendments including raising the compensation cap from $150,000 to $200,000, ending indexation of prior payments, naming non-participating institutions after six months, introducing an advance payment scheme for ill or elderly applicants, and making the government the funder of last resort for institutions that restructure to avoid liability, citing Jehovah’s Witnesses as an example.

The National Redress Scheme Amendment (Technical Amendments) Bill 2020 makes minor and technical changes to increase efficiency and fix oversights; the Morrison government opposed an opposition amendment, noting 191 institutions have joined and a review by Robyn Kruk AO is underway.
